intro: A trumpet call and jagged string figures launch a rondo built from tightly interlocking parts. A slower D-major episode interrupts the counterpoint with a trumpet melody whose turning figure will become important in the finale.
question: When the texture becomes crowded, can you follow one short figure as it moves between instruments?

cues.title: Three gestures become a theme
cues.text: A trumpet gives the first short call; the strings answer with a jagged figure, and further rising gestures complete the opening material. Mahler will combine and separate these cells throughout the movement.
cues.evidence: First-edition score, printed p. 104, shows the successive trumpet, string, horn and wind gestures. The report begins with active sound and substantial attack density; this describes the opening paragraph, not simultaneous attacks.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One strand at a time
cues.text: Choose a short figure and follow its transfers between winds, brass and strings. The counterpoint becomes easier to grasp if you hear several purposeful lines rather than one undifferentiated rush.
cues.evidence: The score’s contrapuntal combination of introductory cells is described by Lew Smoley: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-rondo-burleske-allegro-assai-sehr-trotzig/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Defiance in the score
cues.text: The heading “Sehr trotzig” means very defiant. Short accents, angular intervals and lines that overlap before their predecessors finish make that character concrete; it is not simply an instruction to play fast.
cues.evidence: The movement heading and overlapping construction are visible in the opening score pages. The report shows a persistently active opening stretch, including 3–4 detected attacks per second around 1:25; this is not a beat count.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The lighter subject has relatives
cues.text: The rondo also contains a lighter, strolling subject. Its apparently easier character conceals shared upbeats and figurations from the opening material: contrast need not mean an unrelated tune.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the secondary F-major subject and its derivation from the principal cells. The cue does not claim that its first entry is at 2:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Virtuosity beyond the soloist
cues.text: This movement demands virtuosity from the orchestra as a whole. In his 1936 book, Walter singled out its elaborate counterpoint; his later recording preserves the conductor’s own practical answer to those balancing problems.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay quotes Walter’s description of the movement’s contrapuntal writing: https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: The bass is an argument
cues.text: Listen beneath the quick upper parts for the descending figures and brass statements. In this rondo, a lower line often argues with the melody rather than merely marking the harmony.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the low-brass thematic variants and descending bass phrases within the opening rondo. No individual trombone entrance or pitch is fixed to 3:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A brief change of scale
cues.text: The opening span alternates forceful orchestral statements with lighter textures. A small reduction can reveal the same rhythmic cells in a different character without stopping the movement’s basic momentum.
cues.evidence: The report drops from −11.4 dB at 4:05 to lower windows at 4:10 and 4:20, while detected attacks remain active. The score supplies the alternation of thematic characters.

cues.title: Shared material, different manners
cues.text: When the lighter music returns, compare its little upbeats with the aggressive opening. The notes’ rhythmic placement and orchestral colour can change their manner while preserving their family resemblance.
cues.evidence: Score-based comparison of the recurring principal and secondary subjects, documented in Smoley’s guide. No precise return boundary is assigned to this cue.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A different kind of continuity
cues.text: As the slower lyrical episode approaches, listen for the crowded counterpoint to give way to sustained string sound and a solo trumpet. The new texture makes room for a long line where the opening had crowded together short gestures.
cues.evidence: The score introduces the D-major episode through reduced strings and trumpet. This report’s 5:38 boundary and fall from busy attack counts before 5:30 to sparse counts from 5:35 onward anchor the approaching change.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trumpet’s turning figure
cues.text: In the D-major episode, the trumpet melody circles a note in a small turning figure before making a wider leap. Remember that turn: the finale will give closely related material a much slower, string-led setting.
cues.evidence: The score-derived trumpet melody and finale connection are described by Smoley. Low attack density and D-major-compatible pitch content at 5:35–6:15 locate the lyrical region; no precise note onset is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lyrical does not mean small
cues.text: The lyrical episode grows into one of this recording’s largest crests. Sustained notes can carry as much weight as rapid motion; listen for the contrast between breadth here and the opening’s tightly packed gestures.
cues.evidence: The report’s highest windows are 6:50 and 7:05, with very low detected attack density. The increase follows a strong boundary at 6:34.

cues.title: The episode is interrupted
cues.text: After its crest, the lyrical material meets increasingly pointed interruptions. The E♭ clarinet reshapes the turn into a sharper gesture while fragments of the rondo begin to reappear.
cues.evidence: Smoley documents the clarinet distortion and gradual rondo return. The report drops sharply at 7:10 and marks changes at 7:16, 7:28 and 7:40; the cue covers the interruption region, not a first clarinet attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ten-disc symphony
cues.text: The first commercial issue occupied twenty 78-rpm sides. Contemporary reviewing placed this movement at sides thirteen to fifteen: a complete performance had to be distributed across short physical units, unlike this continuous digital file.
cues.evidence: Pristine PASC389 reproduces the 1939 Gramophone review with movement III on sides 13–15, and lists the ten-disc HMV issue: https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc389 . No audible cut is inferred.

cues.title: Fragments prepare the return
cues.text: In the quieter bridge, listen for brief pieces of the opening material before it returns at full weight. Mahler prepares the recovery through texture and recognition, not simply by restarting the first page.
cues.evidence: The score-derived bridge lets rondo fragments infiltrate the lyrical episode. Strong boundaries at 8:24, 8:36 and 8:54 lead towards rising level and attack density around 9:00–9:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The principal subject returns
cues.text: The forceful rondo material regains the foreground. The lighter strolling subject does not return with it; the remaining span concentrates on the opening cells and their increasingly compressed combinations.
cues.evidence: Smoley distinguishes this final reprise from the earlier alternation. The report rises strongly through 9:00–9:10 and resumes sustained rapid attack density, supporting a broad return around 9:00.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A performance before exile
cues.text: The recording was made in January 1938, two months before the Anschluss. Walter, who was Jewish, then had to leave Austria; the Nazis also removed Mahler’s music from concert programmes under their control.
cues.evidence: Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 2, describes the Anschluss, Walter’s departure and the suppression of Mahler’s music.

cues.title: The score presses faster
cues.text: The closing pages move through “Più stretto” towards “Presto”. The orchestra compresses and repeats the opening gestures, with brass and percussion reinforcing a finish that does not offer the lyrical episode another return.
cues.evidence: Score printed pp. 157–163 includes Più stretto and Presto, dense brass and percussion. The report has late high-level windows at 10:35 and 10:45; these locate the closing drive, not the exact tempo-change bars.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sharp end, then space
cues.text: The movement ends decisively rather than fading into the Adagio. Keep the lyrical episode’s turn figure in mind during the break: its transformation helps connect two movements with very different surfaces.
cues.evidence: The score closes the Rondo-Burleske with sharply articulated orchestral gestures. This file’s level falls after 11:10 and is very low by 11:20; the final cue occupies the post-ending region before the 11:26 file end.

transitions.title: Dense counterpoint yields to a trumpet melody
transitions.how: The opening rondo’s busy lines contract into a reduced texture, with sustained string tremolo and a solo trumpet melody. D major replaces the opening A-minor centre, and the pace broadens. The new melody is connected to earlier material by its turn and leap: Mahler changes the treatment of a figure rather than introducing an unrelated slow piece.
transitions.evidence: The score and Smoley establish the tonal and instrumental change. The local report’s 5:38 boundary, reduced attack density and following D-major-compatible region anchor the approximate join.

transitions.title: The melodic turn becomes a pointed interruption
transitions.how: The episode’s broad crest breaks into separated replies. Clarinets, including the E♭ clarinet, sharpen and compress the lyrical turn, while harp glissandos and string tremolos repeatedly interrupt the attempted recovery of the rondo. The same melodic cell can serve a sustained song or a terse interjection.
transitions.evidence: Score-derived interruption sequence, described by Smoley; the report drops sharply at 7:10 and marks several changes between 7:16 and 7:54. The exact clarinet entrance is unaligned.

transitions.title: Opening fragments recover the full orchestral texture
transitions.how: Fragments of the opening subject accumulate in strings and winds through the bridge. The principal rondo material then returns with low-brass weight and renewed contrapuntal activity. The earlier lighter subject drops out of the design, leaving the first subject’s cells to dominate the approach to the coda.
transitions.evidence: The score supplies the final reprise and omitted secondary subject. Boundaries at 8:36 and 8:54 precede the pronounced rise in level and attack density at 9:00–9:10.

transitions.title: Repetition compresses the material into a faster close
transitions.how: Increasing speed tightens the final reprise into a coda. The score’s “Più stretto” and later “Presto” concentrate the short opening cells in strings, winds and brass, punctuated by percussion. Instead of returning to the D-major episode, Mahler drives the recurring gestures towards the sharply articulated A-minor ending.
transitions.evidence: Score printed pp. 157–163 supplies the tempo directions and close. Sustained activity from 10:00 and high-level windows at 10:35–10:45 locate the coda broadly; its first bar is not timed precisely.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement III, printed pp. 104–163; especially opening and pp. 156–163. Highlights describe successive passage scoring, not a complete or bar-aligned entrance log.

timeline.note: The first short gesture is a solo trumpet call; strings answer immediately afterwards.
Opening paragraph: the jagged string figure and horn call join rising wind and lower-string gestures.
D-major episode: solo trumpet melody above a reduced string texture, with flute colour around the transition.
Interruption region: clarinets reshape the turn; harp and string tremolos separate successive attempts to continue.
Final reprise region: low brass and lower strings reinforce the recovered principal subject.
Closing drive: dense contrapuntal writing with brass, timpani and percussion punctuation; no solo line remains continuously dominant.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
